templates.name: Finite vs nonfinite, finite main verb
Pronoun-antecedent agreement: possessive determiner its/their vs contractions
Subject-verb agreement, quantifier or compound subject
Finite vs nonfinite, finite second or subordinate verb
Plural vs possessive nouns: one- or two-slot spelling grid
Finite vs nonfinite, to-infinitive (purpose or after “the first”)

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (Before + -ing), passage-final blank; a part of the horn, not the animal, is the right subject
items.passage: Pronghorns, grazers of North America’s western grasslands, are the only mammals that annually shed the keratinous outer covering of their horns. Before falling off in late autumn, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: pronghorns grow new keratin over each horn’s bony core, loosening the old sheath.
the loosening of each horn’s old sheath is caused by new keratin growing over the bony core.
it is new keratin growing over each horn’s bony core that loosens the old sheath.
each horn’s old sheath is loosened by new keratin growing over the bony core.
items.explanation: The phrase “Before falling off in late autumn” must describe the thing that falls off, which the first sentence identifies as the keratinous outer covering of the horn. Choice D places “each horn’s old sheath” right after the phrase as the subject, so the sentence correctly says that the sheath is loosened before it falls off.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the animal the passage is about
A.why_wrong: “Pronghorns” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the animals themselves fall off in late autumn.

B.recipe: nominalised subject (N), the key’s noun inside an of-phrase
B.why_wrong: The subject is “the loosening,” not the sheath, so the sentence illogically says that the loosening falls off in late autumn.

C.recipe: expletive opener (E), built on a different noun
C.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, leaving “Before falling off in late autumn” without a noun it can logically describe.

items.notes: Subject: pronghorn horn sheaths (science, zoology). Band-7 settings: the opener describes a part, not the animal the passage is about (the component key b1 used, here with a new opener, Before + -ing, and a passage-final blank as in 188f7e3c); the hardest distractor (A) starts with the obvious noun and keeps every fact; the key’s noun (sheath) is not in the passage, which says “outer covering.” Recipes W, W, E; the expletive is built on “new keratin,” not on the key’s noun. All four options share “new keratin,” the horn’s bony core and its old sheath (after the reviewer’s change, B and D name “each horn’s old sheath” and “the bony core”). Weakest point: the first sentence names the thing that falls off (“outer covering”) before the opener, so a careful reader can match it to “sheath.” Reviewer: B was “new keratin grows ...,” killed at a glance by new versus old; it is now a nominalised subject that carries the key’s noun (the loosening of each horn’s old sheath), as 2bca654a’s “the transport of nutrients,” and the key is recast as an X’s Y subject (each horn’s old sheath). Recipes W, N, E.

fixes: hardened B: “new keratin grows ...” (killed by new versus old) replaced by the nominalised “the loosening of each horn’s old sheath is caused by ...”
key recast as the X’s Y subject “each horn’s old sheath is loosened by ...”; explanation and B rationale updated

band7.why: After the fix, the shape of the band-7 R3 recipe: an X’s Y key (each horn’s old sheath), W with the obvious noun that keeps every fact (pronghorns), N carrying the key’s own noun inside an of-phrase (the loosening of each horn’s old sheath) and E; options 13 to 17 words, all grammatical clauses, key not the longest. Residual weak point, as the writer noted: the first sentence names the covering, so a careful reader knows what falls off; the N option is what keeps that from settling it.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: -ing participial opener with a dash aside, passage-final blank; a compound subject (both rivers) is required
items.passage: Near Manaus, Brazil, two immense rivers converge. Differing in temperature, velocity, and sediment load—the Solimões transports Andean silt, whereas the Rio Negro is darkened by organic compounds from decomposing vegetation—______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the merging of the Solimões and the Rio Negro is delayed for several kilometers.
it takes several kilometers for the waters of the Solimões and the Rio Negro to mix.
the Solimões and the Rio Negro flow side by side for several kilometers before mixing.
a visible boundary between the Solimões and the Rio Negro persists for several kilometers.
items.explanation: “Differing in temperature, velocity, and sediment load” describes two things that differ from each other: the two rivers. Choice C places the compound subject “the Solimões and the Rio Negro” right after the phrase, so the sentence correctly says that the rivers, which differ in these ways, flow side by side before mixing.

A.why_wrong: “The merging” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the merging differs in temperature, velocity, and sediment load.

B.recipe: expletive opener (E), the rivers’ waters inside a for-to clause
B.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, leaving “Differing in temperature, velocity, and sediment load” without a noun it can logically describe.

D.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the boundary
D.why_wrong: “A visible boundary” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the boundary differs in temperature, velocity, and sediment load.

items.notes: Subject: the Meeting of Waters near Manaus (science, hydrology). Band-7 settings from 2bca654a: an -ing opener with a dash aside, a passage-final blank and a compound key (two things acting jointly) against nominalised, expletive and wrong-thing options, none of which names a single river (a single river could arguably “differ”). The expletive is built on “it takes ... for the waters ... to mix,” not on the key’s clause; B also carries “the waters of,” the property noun a student may reach for. Options 14 to 15 words, all sharing the two names and “several kilometers.”

band7.why: Slot for slot the shape of 2bca654a: -ing opener with a dash aside, passage-final blank and a compound key (only the two rivers can differ in temperature, velocity and sediment load), against N (the merging of ...), E (it takes ... for the waters of ... to mix) and W (a visible boundary between ...), each carrying both river names; options 14 to 15 words.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: gerund subject whose object holds plural nouns and a four-name list; be-family options
items.passage: African American choreographer Katherine Dunham was also a trained anthropologist, educated at the University of Chicago. Documenting the ceremonial and social dances of Jamaica, Martinique, Trinidad, and Haiti during ethnographic fieldwork in the mid-1930s ______ fundamental to her development of the Dunham Technique, a movement vocabulary that dance schools still teach.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the gerund phrase “Documenting the ceremonial and social dances of Jamaica, Martinique, Trinidad, and Haiti during ethnographic fieldwork in the mid-1930s,” and a gerund phrase is singular. The singular past tense verb “was” agrees with it and fits a past event.

B.why_wrong: The plural verb “were” doesn’t agree with the singular gerund subject; it agrees only with the nearby plural nouns such as “dances.”

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “are” doesn’t agree with the singular gerund subject “Documenting the ... dances ... mid-1930s.”

D.why_wrong: The plural verb “have been” doesn’t agree with the singular gerund subject “Documenting the ... dances ... mid-1930s.”

items.notes: Subject: Katherine Dunham’s Caribbean fieldwork (arts, dance). Band 6 on c91ef0f0 (gerund subject): 17 words between “Documenting” and the blank, with a plural object (“dances”), a four-name list that reads like a compound subject and a plural-looking “mid-1930s” right before the blank. All three distractors plural. Real person, details well known (University of Chicago anthropology, 1935-36 Caribbean fieldwork, the Dunham Technique).

band7.why: Planned band 6 on c91ef0f0: a gerund subject 17 words before the blank, with a plural object, a four-name list and the plural-looking “mid-1930s” right before the blank; no intervener verb of the other number (the band-7 R1 setting), so a strong band 6.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: main verb after a long subject holding a relative clause, an infinitive and an -ing noun
items.passage: The letters that Afonso I, ruler of the Kingdom of Kongo, dispatched to King João III of Portugal in 1526 to protest the kidnapping of his subjects by Portuguese slave traders ______ among the earliest surviving African denunciations of the transatlantic slave trade.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject “The letters” is followed by a long relative clause (“that Afonso I ... dispatched ... to protest ... traders”), but the sentence still needs a main verb for “The letters.” The finite present tense verb “rank” supplies it.

A.why_wrong: The participle “ranking” doesn’t give the subject “The letters” a finite verb, so the sentence is a fragment.

C.why_wrong: “Having ranked” doesn’t give the subject “The letters” a finite verb, so the sentence is a fragment.

D.why_wrong: The infinitive “to rank” doesn’t give the subject “The letters” a finite verb; it reads as a second purpose phrase after “to protest,” and the sentence has no main verb.

items.notes: Subject: Afonso I of Kongo’s 1526 letters (history). The plan set band 7, but R2_finite_main has no band-7 official items (spec/rw/band7/form_structure_and_sense.md appendix), so this is a strong band 6 with band_target 6. Frame varied from b1 (dash list) and b2 (what-clause): a restrictive relative clause whose own finite verb (“dispatched”) comes early, then an infinitive (“to protest”) and an -ing noun (“kidnapping”) that make the nonfinite options sound continuous; 29 words between the head “letters” and the blank, no commas to mark the end of the subject. Details are standard history (the 1526 letters to João III about Portuguese traders seizing his subjects).

band7.why: R2_finite_main has no band-7 official items (spec/rw/band7/form_structure_and_sense.md appendix), so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6 on a75d5984: 29 words from head to blank holding a relative clause, an infinitive and an -ing noun, with no comma marking the end of the subject.

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: possessive determiner before its singular antecedent, plural nouns before and right after the blank
items.passage: In medieval Europe, fiddles were played with horsehair bows, as violins are today. With ______ strings set vibrating instead by a rosined wooden wheel that the performer rotates with a crank, the hurdy-gurdy, another instrument of that era, can sustain a continuous drone for as long as the wheel keeps revolving.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The blank comes before its antecedent: the phrase “With ______ strings set vibrating instead by a rosined wooden wheel ...” describes “the hurdy-gurdy,” the subject of the main clause. The singular possessive determiner “its” agrees with that singular noun.

A.recipe: contraction for possessive determiner, wrong number
A.why_wrong: “They’re” is a contraction of “they are,” not a possessive, and it is plural, while the strings belong to the singular “hurdy-gurdy.”

B.why_wrong: The plural “their” doesn’t agree with the singular “the hurdy-gurdy”; it can only point back to the fiddles, whose strings are played with bows, not with a wheel.

D.why_wrong: “It’s” is a contraction of “it is,” not a possessive determiner.

items.notes: Subject: the hurdy-gurdy (arts, music). Band-7 settings from 0bcb4417: the determiner comes 16 words before its antecedent, inside a fronted with-phrase (the possessed noun follows directly, as in the model, but the antecedent is singular, varying both models’ “their”); plural nouns sit before the blank (fiddles, bows, violins) and right after it (strings), so “their” is the nearest-noun trap, and the first sentence’s fiddles are logically excluded because their strings are bowed. The 2 x 2 grid (its, it’s, their, they’re).

band7.why: The 0bcb4417 setting: the determiner sits 16 words before its antecedent inside a fronted with-phrase, with plural nouns before (fiddles, bows, violins) and right after (strings) the blank, so “their” reads well until “the hurdy-gurdy” arrives; the 2 x 2 grid of both band-7 officials, with a singular antecedent varying their “their.”

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: compound subject with a contrast tag (X and Y, not Z); every intervening verb and noun in the run singular; options as c7cb5186 (two singular forms, one nonfinite)
items.passage: In Croatia’s Plitvice Lakes, sixteen lakes descend a forested valley in a series of terraces, each held back by a natural barrier of porous travertine. The calcium carbonate that precipitates from the mineral-rich water, settling fastest wherever the current churns and splashes, and the moss that traps this mineral before it can wash downstream, not any ancient landslide, ______ these distinctive barriers.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is compound: “The calcium carbonate that precipitates from the mineral-rich water ... and the moss that traps this mineral ...,” two things joined by “and.” The phrase “not any ancient landslide” is set off by commas and doesn’t change the subject’s number, so the blank needs a plural finite verb: “build.”

A.why_wrong: The singular verb “builds” agrees with the nearby “landslide” or with “moss,” not with the compound subject joined by “and.”

C.why_wrong: The singular verb “has built” doesn’t agree with the compound subject joined by “and.”

D.why_wrong: “Building” has no singular ending, but it isn’t a finite verb: with it, the compound subject never gets a main verb, so the sentence is a fragment.

items.notes: Subject: Plitvice Lakes travertine barriers (science, geology). The reviewer replaced the first subject (why glacier ice looks blue): official Command of Evidence item 8545ccfe explains blue ice by the same bubble-free mechanism. Band-7 settings kept: a plural (compound) key behind singular nouns only (calcium carbonate, water, current, moss, mineral, landslide) and interveners with their own singular verbs (“precipitates,” “churns,” “splashes,” “traps”), as the band-7 recipe asks; the contrast tag as in c7cb5186 with each conjunct long; about 30 words from the first head to the blank; the first conjunct closes with a participial aside set off by a comma pair and ending on an intransitive verb (“splashes”), so no comma falls between the two halves of the subject and “the moss” cannot be misread as a second object of “from,” and the noun right before the blank (“landslide”) is singular. Option set as c7cb5186 (determines, determining, has determined, determine), so a student who settles the number still has two options and must check finiteness. The two compounds already in the bank (w1b4_06, the Bajau item) have no contrast tag. Plain geology, no named study.

fixes: subject replaced: why glacier ice looks blue is explained by the same bubble-free mechanism in official Command of Evidence item 8545ccfe; new passage on Plitvice travertine barriers with the same scaffold (compound subject, not-Z tag, singular nouns and verbs only in the run, register kept at CB’s hard figures)
hardened: “is producing” replaced by the nonfinite “building,” the c7cb5186 option set; explanation, rationales, notes and claims.txt updated

band7.why: c7cb5186’s design with longer conjuncts: compound subject with a not-Z tag, plural key behind singular nouns only, two intervener verbs of the other number (precipitates, churns, splashes, traps); after the fix the option set is c7cb5186’s (two singular finite forms and a nonfinite -ing), so number alone leaves two options and finiteness decides.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head behind a participial phrase holding plural nouns; lexical-verb options
items.passage: The term “Dutch disease,” coined by The Economist in 1977 after soaring natural gas exports appeared to undermine manufacturers in the Netherlands, ______ how a boom in one natural resource can weaken a country’s other export industries.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is the singular noun “term”; the phrase “coined by The Economist ... in the Netherlands” only describes it. The singular verb “describes” agrees with “term.”

A.why_wrong: The plural verb “describe” agrees with nearby plural nouns such as “manufacturers,” not with the singular subject “term.”

B.why_wrong: The plural verb “are describing” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “term.”

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “have described” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “term.”

items.notes: Subject: the term Dutch disease (social science, economics). Medium setting: one participial intervener of 17 words with plural attractors (exports, manufacturers, and “Netherlands” right before the blank). The Economist coined the term in 1977; the Groningen gas boom is the standard account.

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: subject pronoun with a singular antecedent a sentence back, plural rivals between
items.passage: At dusk, many parrotfish species spend up to an hour enclosing themselves in a cocoon of mucus secreted by glands in their gills. Blood-feeding parasites called gnathiid isopods attack reef fishes at night, and researchers in Australia found that ______ can shield sleeping parrotfish from these pests.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun must refer to the thing that shields the sleeping fish: the singular noun “cocoon” in the first sentence. The singular pronoun “it” agrees with “cocoon.”

B.why_wrong: The plural pronoun “they” doesn’t agree with the singular antecedent “cocoon”; the plural nouns nearby, such as “isopods” and “researchers,” can’t be what shields the fish.

C.recipe: right kind of slot, wrong number demonstrative
C.why_wrong: The plural demonstrative “those” doesn’t agree with the singular antecedent “cocoon.”

D.why_wrong: “One” would refer to an unspecified person or thing, not back to the cocoon the passage describes.

items.notes: Subject: parrotfish mucus cocoons and gnathiid isopods (science, marine biology). Medium setting: antecedent one sentence back, with plural rivals between (parasites, isopods, fishes, researchers); the verb after the blank is a modal, so number shows only in the pronoun. Researchers left unnamed (the Lizard Island work).

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (After + -ing), mid-sentence blank; the writer is the right subject
items.passage: After withdrawing from society to the quiet, forested hills surrounding Kyoto, then Japan’s capital, ______ a brief meditation on the impermanence of all things.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the Hōjōki (1212) was written by Japanese poet Kamo no Chōmei as
Japanese poet Kamo no Chōmei wrote the Hōjōki (1212),
Japanese poet Kamo no Chōmei’s Hōjōki (1212) was composed as
a hut is where Japanese poet Kamo no Chōmei wrote the Hōjōki (1212),
items.explanation: Only a person can withdraw from society, so the noun right after the opening phrase must name the writer. Choice B places “Japanese poet Kamo no Chōmei” there, so the sentence correctly says that he withdrew and then wrote the Hōjōki.

A.recipe: passive that leaves the wrong noun as subject (V)
A.why_wrong: “The Hōjōki” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the book withdrew from society.

C.why_wrong: The subject is “Hōjōki,” not Kamo no Chōmei, so the sentence illogically says that the book withdrew from society.

D.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the place
D.why_wrong: “A hut” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the hut withdrew from society.

items.notes: Subject: Kamo no Chōmei’s Hōjōki (literature). Medium setting: a short, clear opener and a plain agent key, as in 2.17. Recipes V, P, W; no it-cleft wrapping the key. Key is the shortest option. Facts are standard (Hōjōki, 1212, written in a small hut in the hills around Kyoto); the reviewer made “southeast of Kyoto” general, since he first withdrew to Ōhara and only later moved to Hino.

fixes: “wooded hills southeast of Kyoto” made general (“forested hills surrounding Kyoto, then Japan’s capital”): Chōmei first withdrew to Ōhara, only later to Hino

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head behind an appositive holding a plural noun and its own plural verb; be-family options
items.passage: A cave pearl, one of the smooth, spherical stones that form in shallow pools beneath dripping water in limestone caverns, ______ composed of concentric layers of calcite precipitated around a tiny nucleus, such as a grain of sand.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is the singular noun “cave pearl”; the phrase between the commas only renames it. The singular verb “is” agrees with “cave pearl.”

A.why_wrong: The plural verb “are” agrees with nearby plural nouns such as “stones” and “caverns,” not with the singular subject “cave pearl.”

B.why_wrong: The plural verb “were” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “cave pearl.”

D.why_wrong: The plural verb “have been” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “cave pearl.”

items.notes: Subject: cave pearls (science, geology). Medium setting from 2.21: an appositive full of plurals (stones, pools, caverns) with its own plural verb “form,” then the blank.

items.subtype: Tense: simple past with a relative-time cue (“Some six centuries later”) and a past relative clause
items.passage: Carolingian minuscule, a legible, rounded script, spread through Europe’s monasteries in the late 700s and the 800s. Some six centuries later, Italian humanists who mistook manuscripts written in it for ancient Roman texts ______ a new script on its letterforms, which early printers later adapted for movable type.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence describes events of the early Renaissance: “Some six centuries later” counts forward from the 700s and 800s, and the other verbs (“mistook,” “adapted”) are in the past tense. The simple past “modeled” fits this past time frame.

B.why_wrong: The future “will model” doesn’t fit events that took place centuries ago, as “mistook” and “adapted” show.

C.recipe: present simple where past is needed
C.why_wrong: The present “model” doesn’t fit the past events the sentence describes.

D.why_wrong: The present progressive “are modeling” suggests an action happening now, not one completed centuries ago.

items.notes: Subject: Carolingian minuscule and the humanist script (history). Medium setting: the time cue is relative (counted from the first sentence’s dates), with past verbs on both sides of the blank. No named humanist.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: second verb of a compound predicate split by a parenthesis
items.passage: Largely self-taught as a composer, American pianist Amy Beach learned orchestration by studying the scores of European masters. She then wrote her “Gaelic” Symphony (a work built on Irish folk melodies) and ______ it premiered by the Boston Symphony Orchestra in 1896.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “And” joins two verbs that share the subject “She”: “wrote” and the verb in the blank. To match the finite past tense verb “wrote,” the blank needs the finite past tense verb “saw.”

A.why_wrong: The participle “seeing” can’t be joined by “and” to the finite verb “wrote” as a second main verb.

B.why_wrong: The infinitive “to see” can’t serve as the second main verb after “wrote ... and.”

C.why_wrong: “Having seen” can’t serve as the second main verb after “wrote ... and.”

items.notes: Subject: Amy Beach’s Gaelic Symphony, premiered by the Boston Symphony Orchestra in 1896 (arts, music). Medium setting from 2.1 (band 6 there): a compound predicate whose two verbs are split by an interrupter, here a parenthesis instead of 2.1’s dash pair.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: main verb after a plural subject and a short interrupter
items.passage: Not every volcano erupts molten rock. The mud volcanoes of Azerbaijan, for example, ______ a mixture of mud, water, and hydrocarbon gases such as methane, which occasionally ignites at the surface.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The second sentence has the subject “The mud volcanoes” but no main verb. The finite verb “release” supplies it.

A.why_wrong: The participle “releasing” doesn’t give the sentence a finite verb.

B.why_wrong: The infinitive “to release” doesn’t give the sentence a finite verb.

D.why_wrong: “Having released” doesn’t give the sentence a finite verb.

items.notes: Subject: Azerbaijan’s mud volcanoes (science, geology). Canonical easy option set.

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: subject pronoun, singular antecedent in the previous sentence
items.passage: The gegenschein (German for “counterglow”) is an oval patch of sunlight scattered by interplanetary dust, visible at the point opposite the Sun. Because ______ is so dim, observers can detect the glow only on moonless nights far from artificial lighting.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun refers back to “the gegenschein,” a singular noun. The singular pronoun “it” agrees with it.

A.why_wrong: The plural pronoun “they” doesn’t agree with the singular antecedent “the gegenschein.”

C.why_wrong: The plural demonstrative “those” doesn’t agree with the singular antecedent “the gegenschein.”

D.why_wrong: “Both” refers to two things, but the passage describes a single glow.

items.notes: Subject: the gegenschein (science, astronomy). Easy setting: the antecedent is the subject of the previous sentence, with no rival noun before the blank.

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: object pronoun, plural antecedent in the previous sentence
items.passage: Polish poet Wisława Szymborska, winner of the 1996 Nobel Prize in Literature, published fewer than 350 poems over a career spanning more than six decades. She polished ______ line by line, often allowing several years to elapse between slim collections.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun refers back to “poems,” the plural noun for what Szymborska published. The plural pronoun “them” agrees with it.

A.why_wrong: The singular pronoun “it” doesn’t agree with the plural antecedent “poems.”

B.why_wrong: The singular demonstrative “this” doesn’t agree with the plural antecedent “poems.”

C.why_wrong: The singular demonstrative “that” doesn’t agree with the plural antecedent “poems.”

items.notes: Subject: Wisława Szymborska’s small output (literature). Option set as in 1.12. Facts are standard (1996 Nobel, fewer than 350 published poems, a new collection every few years).

fixes: “only about 350 poems” changed to the usual “fewer than 350 poems”

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: plural subject (an unfamiliar plural noun) with no intervener; be-family options
items.passage: In the subarctic peatlands of northern Finland and Sweden, palsas ______ low mounds of peat with a core of permanently frozen ground, even where the surrounding bog thaws each summer.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject “palsas” is plural, as the plural “mounds” confirms. The plural verb “are” agrees with it.

B.why_wrong: The singular verb “is” doesn’t agree with the plural subject “palsas.”

C.why_wrong: The singular verb “was” doesn’t agree with the plural subject “palsas.”

D.why_wrong: The singular verb “has been” doesn’t agree with the plural subject “palsas.”

items.notes: Subject: palsas (science, geography). Easy setting from 1.28 (an unfamiliar plural noun, “ayllus”), with the plural confirmed after the blank.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head with a possessive, no intervener; lexical-verb options
items.passage: Sawfishes are rays named for their long, flat snouts, which are lined on both sides with toothlike projections. A sawfish’s snout ______ thousands of tiny pores that detect the faint electrical fields generated by prey hidden in murky water or sediment.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the singular noun “snout.” The singular verb “contains” agrees with it.

A.why_wrong: The plural verb “contain” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “snout.”

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “are containing” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “snout.”

D.why_wrong: The plural verb “have contained” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “snout.”

items.notes: Subject: sawfish electroreception (science, zoology). Easy setting: the subject sits right before the blank; the first sentence’s plural “snouts” is the only pull the other way.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular named subject in a present-tense account of a novel; lexical-verb options
items.passage: Icelandic writer Halldór Laxness won the 1955 Nobel Prize in Literature. In his novel Independent People (1934–1935), the sheep farmer Bjartur ______ his independence above everything else, including the welfare of his own family.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the singular noun phrase “the sheep farmer Bjartur.” The singular verb “values” agrees with it.

A.why_wrong: The plural verb “value” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “the sheep farmer Bjartur.”

B.why_wrong: The plural verb “are valuing” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “the sheep farmer Bjartur.”

D.why_wrong: The plural verb “have valued” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “the sheep farmer Bjartur.”

items.notes: Subject: Laxness’s Independent People (literature). Easy setting; the title’s plural “People” is a light attractor three words before the subject.

items.subtype: Tense: simple present for a habitual action (“Each evening”), parallel with present verbs
items.passage: The prayer plant, a low-growing tropical herb native to Brazil’s rainforests, owes its name to a daily movement known as nyctinasty. Each evening, its leaves ______ upward and press together, resembling a pair of hands folded in prayer; at sunrise, they gradually unfold again.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The passage describes something the plant does every day: “Each evening” marks a repeated action, and the other verbs (“owes,” “press,” “unfold”) are in the present tense. The simple present “fold” fits this habitual action.

A.recipe: simple past where present is needed
A.why_wrong: The past tense “folded” doesn’t fit a movement that still happens every evening, as “owes,” “press,” and “unfold” show.

B.recipe: past perfect where the cue is present
B.why_wrong: The past perfect “had folded” places the action before some past moment, which doesn’t fit a present-day daily habit.

C.why_wrong: The past progressive “were folding” describes an action in progress in the past, not a repeated present one.

items.notes: Subject: the prayer plant’s night folding (science, botany). Easy setting: explicit habitual cue (“Each evening”) and a parallel present verb right after the blank, as in 1.17 and 1.3.

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: singular possessor + plural noun, full 2 x 2 grid
items.passage: Between 1800 and 1805, Brazilian sculptor Antônio Francisco Lisboa, known as Aleijadinho, carved twelve life-size soapstone statues of biblical prophets for a hilltop sanctuary in Congonhas. The figures stand along the low walls flanking the ______, their dramatic gestures seemingly directed at the visitors climbing toward the church.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The steps belong to the single hilltop sanctuary, so “sanctuary’s” needs the singular possessive form. The steps themselves are simply plural, so “steps” takes no apostrophe.

B.recipe: missing apostrophe on the possessor + needless apostrophe on the plain plural
B.why_wrong: “Sanctuaries” is a plain plural rather than a possessive, and “step’s” is a possessive where a plain plural is needed.

C.recipe: needless apostrophe on the plain plural
C.why_wrong: “Sanctuary’s” is correct, but “step’s” is a possessive where the plain plural “steps” is needed.

D.why_wrong: “Sanctuaries’” is a plural possessive, but the statues were carved for a single sanctuary.

items.notes: Subject: Aleijadinho’s prophets at Congonhas (arts, sculpture). Number cue for the possessor: “a hilltop sanctuary.” Avoids the bank’s frequent “Many of the ______” frame. Facts are standard (twelve soapstone prophets, 1800 to 1805, Sanctuary of Bom Jesus de Matosinhos).

fixes: “directed at visitors as they ascend” changed to “directed at the visitors climbing toward the church” (“they” could point back to the figures)

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: to-infinitive of purpose after a complete clause
items.passage: American linguist Arnold Zwicky coined the term “recency illusion” in 2005 ______ a widespread misconception: the assumption that a linguistic usage one has only recently noticed must itself be a recent innovation.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause “Arnold Zwicky coined the term ... in 2005” is already complete. The infinitive “to describe” begins a phrase that gives his purpose in coining the term.

A.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
A.why_wrong: The finite verb “described” would be a second main verb for “Arnold Zwicky” with no conjunction joining it to “coined.”

B.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
B.why_wrong: The finite verb “describes” can’t follow the complete clause without a conjunction or a subject of its own.

D.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
D.why_wrong: The finite verb “has described” can’t follow the complete clause without a conjunction or a subject of its own.

items.notes: Subject: Arnold Zwicky’s recency illusion (social science, linguistics). Canonical purpose-infinitive set (1.27: has studied, to study, studied, studies). Zwicky coined the term on Language Log in 2005.

items.subtype: Tense: past perfect for an action continuing up to a dated past event (“By then”)
items.passage: In the 1020s, the government of China’s Song dynasty began issuing paper money in Sichuan. By then, Chinese merchants ______ paper certificates known as “flying cash” to transfer funds between distant cities for about two centuries.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “By then” refers to the 1020s, a past moment, and the merchants’ use of flying cash came before that moment and lasted up to it. The past perfect “had used” shows an action completed before another past event.

A.recipe: present simple where past perfect is needed
A.why_wrong: The present “use” doesn’t fit an action that ended in the past before the 1020s.

C.why_wrong: The future “will use” doesn’t fit an action that had already gone on for two centuries by the 1020s.

D.why_wrong: The present progressive “are using” describes an action happening now, not one that came before the 1020s.

items.notes: Subject: Tang flying cash before Song paper money (history). Easy setting from 1.24: the earlier past is fixed by an explicit cue (“By then” after a dated sentence). No simple past option, so the past perfect is the only defensible form.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: second verb of a compound predicate
items.passage: In his 1989 book The Great Good Place, American sociologist Ray Oldenburg called cafés, pubs, bookstores, and other informal gathering spots “third places,” distinct from the first and second places of home and work, and ______ that such places help hold communities together.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “And” joins two verbs that share the subject “Ray Oldenburg”: “called” and the verb in the blank. To match the finite past tense verb “called,” the blank needs the finite past tense verb “argued.”

B.why_wrong: The participle “arguing” can’t be joined by “and” to the finite verb “called” as a second main verb.

C.why_wrong: The infinitive “to argue” can’t serve as the second main verb after “called ... and.”

D.why_wrong: “Having argued” can’t serve as the second main verb after “called ... and.”

items.notes: Subject: Ray Oldenburg’s third places (social science, sociology). Compound predicate as in 1.11; the first conjunct carries an adjective phrase (“distinct from ...”), not a participle, so “arguing” has nothing to pair with.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: -ing participial phrase after a complete clause and a comma
items.passage: Singapore’s hawkers, vendors of inexpensive cooked food, once operated from pushcarts and makeshift stalls along the city’s streets. From the early 1970s to the mid-1980s, the government relocated them to purpose-built hawker centers, ______ the vendors with running water, drainage, and sanitation facilities the streets had lacked.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause “the government relocated them to purpose-built hawker centers” is complete. After the comma, the participle “providing” begins a phrase that tells what the move did, without creating a second independent clause.

A.recipe: comma splice via pronoun + finite verb
A.why_wrong: “This provided” makes a second independent clause joined to the first with only a comma, a comma splice.

B.recipe: comma splice via pronoun + finite verb
B.why_wrong: “It provided” makes a second independent clause joined to the first with only a comma, a comma splice.

C.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
C.why_wrong: The finite verb “provides” has no subject of its own after the comma, and its present tense doesn’t fit the past events.

items.notes: Subject: Singapore’s hawker centers (social science, urban policy). Option set as in 1.29 (ensuring, this will ensure, ensures, it ensures).
